options: Choosing which cloud provider to train a model on
Transforming or combining raw data into new input variables that make it easier for a model to learn useful patterns
The process of removing all features before training
Writing the model's training loop from scratch
questions.explain: Feature engineering is the practice of deriving new, more informative columns from raw data so the pattern a model needs is more directly exposed to it.

questions.q: In the lesson's example, why is `tickets_per_year` often a stronger churn signal than the raw `total_support_tickets` count?
options: It always has a smaller numeric value
It accounts for how long the customer has had the opportunity to file tickets, distinguishing 7 tickets in 3 months from 7 tickets in 3 years
It removes the need for a label entirely
Raw counts can never be used as features
questions.explain: The raw ticket count alone can't distinguish a brand-new customer filing many tickets quickly from a long-tenured customer filing the same number slowly — normalizing by tenure exposes that difference directly.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of the "date/time decomposition" feature engineering pattern?
options: Dropping a column entirely
Computing price divided by square footage
Extracting day_of_week or is_weekend from a single timestamp column
Averaging every customer's transactions into one row
questions.explain: Date/time decomposition pulls structured, numerically meaningful pieces (like day of week or month) out of a raw timestamp, which a model can't use directly as meaningful numbers on its own.

questions.q: Why can a simple model with well-engineered features often outperform a sophisticated model fed only raw columns?
options: Sophisticated models cannot process numeric data
No algorithm can recover a relationship that was never exposed in the input data in the first place
Simple models always train faster, which is the only advantage
Feature engineering is required by every ML library
questions.explain: If a useful relationship (like tickets normalized by tenure) isn't present in the raw columns at all, even a powerful model has to approximately rediscover it from noisy data — exposing it directly as a feature makes the job far easier.

questions.q: Turning a continuous `days_since_login` value into a binary `is_recently_active` flag (under 30 days) is an example of which pattern?
options: Aggregation
Binning/thresholding
Date decomposition
Ratio/rate normalization
questions.explain: Binning converts a continuous value into a meaningful categorical or binary flag based on a threshold, which is exactly what turning "days since login" into an active/inactive flag does.
